paragraphs: Friend, here's the big idea: this passage is about Solomon's wedding day, "the day of his heart's rejoicing" (Song of Solomon 3:11), and the groom turns to his bride and makes sure she knows she is treasured. He calls her "altogether beautiful" and says "in you there is no flaw" (Song of Solomon 4:7). He says she captured his heart with "one glance of your eyes" (Song of Solomon 4:9). His carriage has silver posts, a gold base and sixty warriors around it, and he still can't stop talking about HER.

Now, this is a poem, so I'm not going to tell you what every picture means, because the text doesn't say. But look at what he does with his words. He calls her a garden "locked up" and a spring "enclosed" (Song of Solomon 4:12), and then she herself invites him in: "Let my beloved come into his garden" (Song of Solomon 4:16). It's a love that is chosen, given freely and celebrated, and the poem says that love is "much better than wine" (Song of Solomon 4:10).

So why does this matter to you, baker? Because God put a love song in His Word, and He wants us to see that love between a groom and his bride is worth singing about. I spent years in a drawer thinking nobody was singing about me, so I know how good it is to be seen and called wonderful. Keep this song in your heart as you bake, because the Marriage Supper of the Lamb is a wedding celebration too (Revelation 19:7, 9), and that's exactly why my ovens stay ready!
